Lieutenant Governor

Democrat

Fiona Ma

Elect Fiona Ma for Lieutenant Governor to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Endorsements: Ma has the endorsement of many groups, including California Young Democrats, Asian Dems of LA, Alice B. Toklas Democratic Club, Equality California, National Union of Healthcare Workers, UNITE HERE Local 11, California Federation of Labor Unions, and United Domestic Workers. She is also supported by U.S. Sens Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis, Secretary of State Shirley Weber, State Controller Malia Cohen, and many other state and local elected officials. Ma has the endorsement of several problematic stakeholders, like the Peace Officers Research Association of California, State Coalition of Probation Organizations, and California Association of Highway Patrolmen. 

Governance and community leadership experience: Ma has been the California treasurer since 2019, when she was elected with 64% of the vote. She previously served on the California State Board of Equalization from 2014–2019, the California State Assembly from 2006–2012 (as speaker from 2010–2012 and majority whip from 2006–2010), and the San Francisco Board of Supervisors from 2002–2006. Ma was also a field representative for then State Assemblymember John Burton. Prior to public service, Ma was an accountant with her own practice. 

Other background: Ma is the daughter of Chinese immigrants, who were a small-business owner and a teacher. She attended Rochester Institute of Technology. 

The Race

June 2 primary election results: State Treasurer Fiona Ma (D) 19%, Gloria Romero (R) 18%, Josh Fryday (D) 15%, Michael Tubbs (D) 13%, Oliver Ma (D) 7%, David Collenberg (R) 7%, David Fennell (R) 6%, and Janelle Kellman (D) 4%. Ten additional candidates each won less than 4% of the vote. Fiona Ma and Gloria Romero will contend in the November 3 general election.

Candidate’s fundraising and pledges: Ma’s campaign has raised $3.4 million and is not funded by fossil fuel or real estate contributions. Her problematic donors include Comcast, Peace Officers Research Association of California, California Correctional Peace Officers Association, and Association for Los Angeles Deputy Sheriffs, and Los Angeles Police Protective League. 

Opposing candidate’s fundraising and pledges: Romero’s campaign has raised $256,035 and is not funded by fossil fuel, police, real estate, or corporate contributions. She has partially self-funded her campaign.

The District

State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position

Lieutenant governors serve as the second-highest executive officer of a state. They are responsible for acting as governor in the case that the sitting governor is temporarily absent, incapacitated, or removed from office, and have additional responsibilities that vary by state. In California, this position chairs the Commission for Economic Development and the State Lands Commission, and provides guidance to the governor on issues across state policy. The lieutenant governor serves as president of the state Senate, and casts a vote in the case of a tie. The lieutenant governor also holds a variety of leadership roles, including as a voting member of the Board of Regents of the University of California, and the Board of Trustees of the California University System. 

Each lieutenant governor is elected by popular vote in a statewide election. In California, lieutenant governors are elected to serve a four-year term, and are limited to two terms in office.

Attorney General

Endorsed by Courage California

Democrat

Rob Bonta

Courage California endorses Attorney General Rob Bonta for re-election to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Progressive endorsements: Attorney General Rob Bonta has the endorsement of many groups in the state, including Courage California, Smart Justice California, California Environmental Voters, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, Equality California, Sierra Club, Teamsters California, and many other labor unions. He has also received the endorsement of Dolores Huerta and many elected officials, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, Sen. Adam Schiff, Sen. Alex Padilla, most members of the Democratic California House delegation, and many state legislators. 

Top issues: Protecting California’s federal funding, fighting organized crime, access to reproductive health care, and maintaining safety and affordability for Californians.

Priority policies: This year, Attorney General Bonta’s priorities for California have focused on efforts to fight the Trump administration’s policies, including blocking an executive order to restrict mail voting, protecting access to gender-affirming care, opposing mandatory immigration detention without due process, and challenging HUD-funding restrictions. His office has also worked to improve the use of sexual assault evidence kits, increase accountability for Big Oil, and block corporate mergers. His office recently brought charges against a fraud ring responsible for $267 million in hospice fraud in Los Angeles, secured significant prison sentences for child sex abusers, and supported litigation that eventually led to the Trump administration dropping their appeals in cases related to rescinding funding from state energy and HUD programs.

Governance and community leadership experience: Attorney General Bonta was first elected to the State Assembly in 2012 and served as a consistent progressive champion for nine years. In 2021, Governor Gavin Newsom appointed him as state attorney general after the seat was vacated by Xavier Becerra upon his confirmation to serve in the Biden administration. Bonta won a full term in the general election in 2022 after defeating his Republican challenger by 18 points.

During his time in the State Assembly, Attorney General Bonta was an effective legislator who worked on bills related to climate protections, criminal justice and prison reform, immigrant rights, and housing protections. Bonta scored a lifetime score of 98 out of 100 on Courage Score, our annual analysis of legislators’ progressive voting records. Based on our Courage Score analysis, he supported the most progressive bills that made it to a vote and earned the Courage Score All-Star designation three times. 
Prior to his election to the State Assembly, Attorney General Bonta served as a deputy city attorney for both the City and County of San Francisco, as an elected member of the Alameda Health Care District Board of Directors, as board president for the Social Service Human Relations board, as board president for Alternatives in Action, and as chair of the Economic Development Commission. He is a longtime activist in the ongoing fight for racial, economic, and social justice.

Other background: Attorney General Rob Bonta, a civil rights attorney, is from Alameda, CA. He is the son of farmworkers who provided leadership to the labor movement and is the first Filipino American to serve as California’s attorney general.

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Attorney General Rob Bonta (D - incumbent) 57%, Michael Gates (R) 38%, and Marjorie Mikels (GRN) 5%. Rob Bonta and Michael Gates will contend in the November 3 general election.

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Attorney General Rob Bonta’s campaign has raised $8.2 million as of August 2026. He is not funded by fossil fuel or police interests. 

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Michael Gates’s campaign has raised $1.4 million as of August 2026, and is not funded by fossil fuel or corporate PAC interests.

The District
State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position
The state attorney general acts as the lead attorney and law-enforcement official for the state of California and has oversight of over 4,500 state-employed district attorneys, investigators, police officers, and administrators. The attorney general executes a variety of responsibilities in the state, including representing the people of California in criminal and civil matters in court, coordinating statewide law-enforcement efforts, providing legal counsel to state agencies, and managing special projects to protect the rights of Californians. California has 58 elected district attorneys who report to the attorney general, one for every county in the state. The attorney general is elected for a four-year term and may serve a maximum of two terms in office. This office has traditionally been held by Democrats.

Re-elect Secretary of State Dr. Shirley Weber to keep California on the right track for progress.

Progressive endorsements: Secretary Weber has the endorsement of many groups, including California Nurses Association, California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, San Diego Democrats for Equality, California Women’s List, and several other labor unions. She has also received the support of several local and state leaders, including Attorney General Rob Bonta, State Controller Malia Cohen, State Superintendent Tony Thurmond, Asm. LaShae Sharp-Collins, and San Diego County Supervisor Monica Montgomery-Steppe. 

Top issues and priority policies: Restoring trust and transparency, encouraging Californians to vote, expanding access to the ballot, monitoring and upgrading cybersecurity policies to protect elections, and revamping voter-education outreach programs for the formerly incarcerated who are now eligible to vote.

Governance experience: Dr. Weber was appointed to serve as secretary of state by Governor Gavin Newsom in 2020 after Alex Padilla was appointed to serve the rest of Vice President Kamala Harris’s Senate term. She was unanimously confirmed by the state legislature. Dr. Weber won her 2022 election with 59% of the vote. She is the first Black California Secretary of State. In this role, Dr. Weber has focused on expanding voter outreach in rural communities and on high school and college campuses. She has sued local governments for violating election laws, successfully defended against the Trump administration’s attempt to seize California’s voter data, and supported the Prop 50 redistricting effort to counter the Republican-led undemocratic gerrymandering campaigns. Community groups have advocated for Dr. Weber to continue to expand access to voters with disabilities and voters with limited English proficiency. 

Dr. Weber previously served in the State Assembly from 2012–2021, and sponsored bills on a variety of issues, including school safety, full-day kindergarten, reducing the use of deadly force by police, strengthening the CalFresh program, and creating the state Reparations Task Force. Her successes also included environmental cleanup, increasing food access for food-insecure communities, establishing protections for residents of long-term nursing facilities, and lowering the cost of childcare. She scored a lifetime 93 out of 100 on Courage Score, our annual analysis of legislators’ progressive voting records. Based on our Courage Score analysis, Sec. Weber supported nearly all progressive bills that made it to a vote. 

Prior to serving in public office, Secretary Weber founded the Department of Africana Studies at San Diego State University in 1972, and taught there for forty years. She also served as president of the National Council for Black Studies from 2002–2006, as president of the San Diego Board of Education from 1988–1996, and as chairperson of San Diego’s Citizens Equal Opportunity Commission. 

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Secretary Dr. Shirley Weber (D - incumbent) 59%, Donald Wagner (R) 37%, Michael Feinstein (GRN) 2%, and Gary Blenner (GRN) 2%. Dr. Shirley Weber and Donald Wagner will contend in the November 3 general election.

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Secretary Weber’s campaign has raised $756,000 as of August 2026, and is not funded by fossil fuel, real estate, or corporate contributions. 

Opposing candidate’s fundraising and pledges: Donald Wagner’s campaign has raised $649,000 as of August 2026, and is funded by law enforcement. Wagner is an Orange County supervisor and a founder of the county’s Federalist Society, a conservative legal group that has successfully gotten more right-wing judges appointed around the country, including to the U.S. Supreme Court. He supports Proposition 39, the Republican-backed ballot measure that will keep eligible Californians from voting, and says he will end the practice of sending mail-in ballots to every voter in the state. 

The District
State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the Governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position
The secretary of state acts as the lead records officer for the state of California, and manages an office of 500 civil-service employees who are responsible for ensuring transparency and accessibility in elections, campaigning, business records, and legislative advocacy. The secretary of state’s office has a significant responsibility for election implementation and integrity, as it produces information pamphlets for voters in ten languages, provides statewide testing and approval for voting equipment, maintains the voter database, and certifies the official candidate lists and the official election results. The secretary of state’s office also oversees the filing and disclosure of campaign-finance information, the management of business records, the safeguarding of statewide address confidentiality, and the maintenance of registries for domestic partnerships and advanced health-care directives. The secretary of state is elected for a four-year term and may serve a maximum of two terms in office. This office has traditionally been held by Democrats.

State Treasurer

Democrat

Eleni Kounalakis

Elect Eleni Kounalakis for Treasurer to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Progressive endorsements: Kounalakis has the endorsement of a many groups, including California Federation of Labor Unions, California Teachers Association, Equality California, California Environmental Voters, Reproductive Freedom for All, UNITE HERE California, National Union of Healthcare Workers, East Area Progressive Democrats, and Teamsters California.

Governance experience: Kounalakis currently serves as California’s lieutenant governor, and was elected to that seat in 2018 with over 56% of the vote. In 2022, she won her re-election against a Republican challenger by 18 points. During her time in state leadership, she has championed bills to improve environmental protections, international affairs, and equity across the state. She has supported efforts to decommission oil drilling, transition the state to renewable energy, reduce carbon emissions, promote California’s economy on the global stage, and establish the first Transgender Advisory Council in the country. She also serves as a member of the University of California Board of Regents and the California State University Board of Trustees, and has advocated for more affordable tuition and creating more affordable student housing on campus. Before holding elected office, she served under Gov. Jerry Brown as chair of the California Advisory Council for International Trade and Investment, was a fellow at the U.S. Department of State’s Bureau of Intelligence and Research, and served as U.S. ambassador to the Republic of Hungary under former President Barack Obama. Before her public service, Kounalakis was a businessperson who served as president of AKT Development, a housing- and land-development firm founded by her father. The firm is the largest in the Sacramento area, and primarily focuses on residential master-planned communities. 

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Lt. Governor Eleni Kounalakis (D) 37%, Jennifer Hawks (R) 24%, Anna Caballero (D) 16%, David Serpa (R) 13%, Tony Vazquez (D) 7%, and Glenn Turner (GRN) 3%. Eleni Kounalakis and Jennifer Hawks will contend in the November 3 general election.

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Eleni Kounalakis’s campaign has raised $668,000 as of August 2026, and is not funded by fossil fuel interests. Her problematic donors include Google, California Statewide Law Enforcement Association PAC, and California Apartment Association PAC.

Opposing candidate fundraising and pledges: Jennifer Hawks’ campaign has raised $79,000 as of August 2026, and is not funded by police, fossil fuel, real estate, or corporate PAC interests.

The District
State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position
Treasurers serve as a state’s chief banker, overseeing revenue and finances for schools, roads, housing, levees, public-health facilities, and infrastructure projects. They can be responsible for pension administration, public employee payroll, and fraud oversight. Treasurers manage the state’s investments and the sale of state bonds, and serve as the trustee of the state’s debt portfolio. In California, the state treasurer manages the banking for the world’s fifth-largest economy and typically oversees around $2.5 trillion in banking transactions during each fiscal year. 

The California state treasurer is elected by popular vote in a statewide election. The state treasurer is elected to serve four-year terms, and is limited to two terms in office.

State Controller

Democrat

Malia Cohen

Re-elect Controller Malia Cohen to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Progressive endorsements: Cohen has the endorsement of many groups, including Equality California, California Environmental Voters, California Nurses Association, SEIU California, California Labor Federation, and several other labor unions. She is also supported by elected leaders, including Senator Adam Schiff, Governor Gavin Newsom, State Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, and Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón. 

Governance experience: Cohen has been state controller since 2023, when she was elected with 55% of the vote. In her tenure as controller, she has prioritized fairness and equity, supporting gender equity, workforce training and development, affordable housing, affordable and quality health care, climate change, and corporate accountability in her duties. Controller Cohen previously served on the California State Board of Equalization and the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. As chair of the San Francisco Employee Retirement System, she led the effort to divest from fossil fuels. 

The Race
Primary election: Controller Malia Cohen (D - incumbent) 57%, Herb Morgan (R) 38%, and Meghann Adams (PF) 6%. Malia Cohen and Herb Morgan will contend in the November 3 general election.

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Controller Malia Cohen’s campaign has raised $2,257,000 as of August 2026, and is funded by police, corporate PAC, and real estate interests.

Opposing candidate’s fundraising and pledges: Herb Morgan’s campaign has raised $557,000 as of August 2026, and is partially self-funded. He does not have any contributions from fossil fuel, real estate, law enforcement, or corporate donors.

The District
State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position
The state controller acts as the lead fiscal authority for the state of California, which is the fifth-largest economy in the world. The state controller manages an office of 1,400 public servants responsible for the disbursement of financial resources across the state. The state controller’s office oversees audits of funds distributed to state agencies and programs, acts as a steward for unclaimed property that falls to state possession, provides accounting and reporting services for government entities, and manages payroll accounting and data for state employees. The state controller also serves as a policy liaison to a variety of finance organizations, including the state’s two pension funds, CalPERS and CalSTRS, and the California Franchise Tax Board. The state controller is elected for a four-year term and may serve a maximum of two terms in office. This office has traditionally been held by Democrats.

Insurance Commissioner

No Recommendation

We recommend that you choose the Democratic candidate who best aligns to your values in this race. 

Ben Allen has been a state Senator since 2014, and won his 2022 re-election with 67% of the vote. This session, Sen. Allen’s priorities for SD-24 include 38 bills about wildfire recovery, environmental protection, green energy, affordable housing, public safety, and campaign-finance reform. Of these, sixteen were successfully chaptered into law. He sponsored and passed legislation to expedite insurance payments and provide tax relief for wildfire survivors, supports electric vehicle chargers for HOA residents, and — if California voters approve the ballot measure on the November 2026 election — will allow public financing of election campaigns to fight against money in politics. He scores a lifetime 91 out of 100 on Courage Score, our annual analysis of legislators’ progressive voting records. Based on our Courage Score analysis, Sen. Allen supported most progressive bills that made it to a vote, and earned the designation of Honorable Mention this year. 

Sen. Allen’s priorities for this position are stabilizing the insurance market, ensuring that Californians receive fair treatment from insurers after disasters, making the Department of Insurance more transparent and accountable, and getting people off the state-run FAIR Plan insurer of last resort. He is endorsed by many groups, including California Environmental Voters, California Federation of Teachers, California Professional Firefighters, Jane Fonda Climate PAC, California Democratic Renters Council, East Area Progressive Democrats, United Auto Workers, and several other labor unions and democratic clubs. Sen. Allen is also supported by many community and elected leaders, such as U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, Rep. Judy Chu, Senate President Pro Tem Monique Limón, Legislative Progressive Caucus Chair Asm. Alex Lee, Los Angeles City Council Member Hugo Soto-Martinez, and several city councilmembers, mayors, school board trustees, and Democratic party chairs. 

Jane Kim served as the California Director for the Working Families Party from 2022-2026, helping to elect more progressive candidates at every level of office in the state and supporting co-governance between elected leaders and communities. She was previously California Political Director for Bernie 2020, San Francisco Supervisor from 2011–2019, and member of the San Francisco Unified Board of Education from 2007–2011. As supervisor, Kim championed policies to make San Francisco the only city in the nation to provide tuition-free community college for all residents, raise the minimum wage, establish a medical respite shelter, invest in childcare through a commercial real estate tax, and tenant protections to prevent unjust evictions. 

Her priorities for this position are lowering insurance costs; ending price discrimination; guaranteeing coverage, including Medicare for Kids; ensuring fast and fair insurance claims; and holding bad actors accountable. Kim is endorsed by several groups, including California Working Families Party, Our Revolution, California Young Democrats, SEIU California, California Teachers Association, National Union of Healthcare Workers, United Domestic Workers, and other labor unions. She is also supported by many community and elected leaders, such as Dolores Huerta, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, State Controller Malia Cohen, Rep. Pramila Jayapal, Rep. Ro Khanna, Rep. Lateefah Simon, Sen. Lena Gonzalez, Asm. Sade Elhawary, San Diego Supervisor Paloma Aguirre, Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas, and several county supervisors, city councilmembers, mayors, and school board trustees. 

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Jane Kim (D) 27%, Ben Allen (D) 19%, Stacy Korsgaden (R) 16%, Robert Howell (R) 8%, Patrick Wolff (D) 7%, Merritt Farren (R) 7%, Steven Bradford (D) 5%, Eric Aarnio (R) 2%. Jane Kim and Ben Allen will contend in the November 3 general election. 

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Allen’s campaign has raised $1.4 million and is funded by police, corporate PAC, and real estate interests. His problematic donors include Disney, California Statewide Law Enforcement PAC, and California Apartment Association. 

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Kim’s campaign has raised $1 million and is not funded by fossil fuel, real estate, law enforcement, or corporate contributions. 

The District
State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position
The state insurance commissioner acts as head of the Department of Insurance, a consumer-protection agency that regulates the state’s insurance marketplace. The commissioner directs the Department of Insurance to ensure that Californians receive fair and indiscriminate insurance rates, timely claim payments, regulated brokerage, and effective complaint and fraud investigations. The insurance commissioner leads a department of 1,400 employees and provides oversight to over 450,000 insurance industry professionals. The Department of Insurance routinely recovers over $84 million for consumers annually.

Kim is endorsed by several groups, including California Working Families Party, Our Revolution, California Young Democrats, SEIU California, California Teachers Association, National Union of Healthcare Workers, United Domestic Workers, and other labor unions. She is also supported by many community and elected leaders, such as Dolores Huerta, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, State Controller Malia Cohen, Rep. Pramila Jayapal, Rep. Ro Khanna, Rep. Lateefah Simon, Sen. Lena Gonzalez, Asm. Sade Elhawary, San Diego Supervisor Paloma Aguirre, Alameda County Supervisor Nikki Fortunato Bas, and several county supervisors, city councilmembers, mayors, and school board trustees. 

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Jane Kim (D) 27%, Ben Allen (D) 19%, Stacy Korsgaden (R) 16%, Robert Howell (R) 8%, Patrick Wolff (D) 7%, Merritt Farren (R) 7%, Steven Bradford (D) 5%, Eric Aarnio (R) 2%. Jane Kim and Ben Allen will contend in the November 3 general election. 

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Allen’s campaign has raised $1.4 million and is funded by police, corporate PAC, and real estate interests. His problematic donors include Disney, California Statewide Law Enforcement PAC, and California Apartment Association. 

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Kim’s campaign has raised $1 million and is not funded by fossil fuel, real estate, law enforcement, or corporate contributions. 

The District
State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position
The state insurance commissioner acts as head of the Department of Insurance, a consumer-protection agency that regulates the state’s insurance marketplace. The commissioner directs the Department of Insurance to ensure that Californians receive fair and indiscriminate insurance rates, timely claim payments, regulated brokerage, and effective complaint and fraud investigations. The insurance commissioner leads a department of 1,400 employees and provides oversight to over 450,000 insurance industry professionals. The Department of Insurance routinely recovers over $84 million for consumers annually.

Superintendent of Public Instruction

Non-Partisan

Richard Barrera

Elect Richard Barrera for State Superintendent to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Progressive endorsements: Barrera is endorsed by many groups, including California Teachers Association, United Administrators Southern California, Latino Democrats of San Francisco, San Diego Democrats for Equality, East Area Progressive Democrats of Los Angeles, and United Domestic Workers. Barrera is also supported by many elected leaders, such as State Superintendent Tony Thurmond, Rep. Juan Vargas, San Diego County Treasurer Larry Cohen, San Diego County Supervisor Terra Lawson-Remer, and several city councilmembers, and school board members and trustees. He has the problematic endorsement of the San Diego Unified Police Officers Association.  

Top priorities: Building a strong, sustainable teacher pipeline; expanding early-childhood education; secure, sustainable funding for stronger schools; empowering communities to fund their schools; making housing affordable for educators; building schools where every student belongs; prioritizing mental health in every school; and delivering equity. 

Governance experience: Barrera has been a member of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education since 2008, and serves as its president. He has led efforts to pass four major school bonds and a first-in-the-nation affordable housing initiative for educators. 

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Sonja Shaw 23%, Richard Barrera 20%, Nichelle Henderson 10%, Wendy Castaneda Leal 9%, Al Muratsuchi 8%, Anthony Rendon 8%, Frank Lara 8%,  Josh Newman 7%, Ainye Long 6%, and Gus Mattammal 2%. Sonja Shaw and Richard Barrera will contend in the November 3 general election. This is a nonpartisan race. 

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Barrera’s campaign has raised $614,000, and is not funded by fossil fuel, real estate, or corporate donors. 

Opposing candidate’s fundraising and pledges: Shaw’s campaign has raised $494,000 and is funded by real estate interests and several conservative groups, including Southern California Area Republican Women, Santa Barbara County Republican Party, and Conservative Patriots of Orange County. Shaw is school board president for the Chino Valley Unified School District and has been a strong supporter of MAGA issues, including banning transgender girls from participating in sports, policing the books allowed in school libraries, and eliminating LGBTQ+ content from classrooms.

The District
State: California is the most populous state in the United States, and includes 58 counties and 40 million residents.

Voter registration: Of the 23 million registered voters in the state, 45% are Democrat, 25% are Republican, and 23% have no party preference. Democrats have held the governor’s seat since 2011.

District demographics: 41% Latino, 17% Asian, and 6% Black.

Recent election results: California voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by 20 points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by 18 points.

The Position
The state superintendent of public instruction serves as a nonpartisan, public advocate for the over 6 million students in public schools. They can bring attention to significant issues affecting the education landscape, and use their influence to urge legislative or policy action within the state. Superintendents hold a constitutionally elected position and are limited to two terms or eight years in office.

Board of Equalization, District 1

Elect Nelson Esparza to the Board of Equalization to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Nelson Esparza is an educator and has served on the Fresno City Council since 2019, and won his 2022 re-election by 43 points. In this role, he has prioritized increasing public safety, bringing affordable housing to the inner city, supporting working families and ensuring equitable infrastructure investments across Fresno. Esparza is a member of the Fresno County Economic Development Corporation Board; is PAC chair of the State Center Federation of Teachers, Local 1533; and serves the Democratic Party. He previously served as a trustee on the Fresno County Board of Education. Esparza has the endorsement of several groups, including Fresno County Young Democrats, San Bernardino County Young Democrats, California Teachers Association, SEIU California, and California Democratic Party. He is also supported by elected leaders, such as California State Controller Malia Cohen, U.S. Sen. Adam Schiff, Rep. Jim Costa, Rep. Adam Gray, BOE Member Sally Lieber, and Asm. Esmeralda Soria. 

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Shannon Grove (R) 35%, Nelson Esparza (D) 34%, Donald Williamson (D) 15%, Dusty Beach (R) 12%, and Nader Shahatit (R) 4%. Shannon Grove and Nelson Esparza will contend in the November 3 general election.

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Nelson Esparza’s campaign has raised $295,000 and is not funded by fossil fuel, law enforcement, or corporate donors.

Opposing candidate’s fundraising and pledges: Shannon Grove’s campaign has raised $1.9 million. Her problematic donors include AT&T, Phillips 66, Amazon, and California Correctional Peace Officers Association.

The District
Counties in district: California’s Board of Equalization District 1 includes 33 inland counties spanning from Modoc and Shasta Counties to the north to San Bernardino County in the south.

Voter registration: 37% Democrat, 33% Republican, and 21% No Party Preference. Republicans typically hold this district.

Recent election results: BOE District 1 voted for Donald Trump for president in 2024 by three points and Brian Dahle for governor in 2022 by eight points.

The Position
The California Board of Equalization is composed of four members elected by popular vote to represent individual districts within the state. It is the only elected tax board in the country. The state controller serves in an at-large capacity as the 5th member. The Board of Equalization is responsible for managing taxation in the state, including in the areas of property, alcoholic beverage, and insurance. This includes oversight of valuation assessments on public utility and railroad property, mapping and assigning tax rates to geographic areas in the state, conducting assessment surveys and compliance audits, and administering tax exemptions. In California, board members meet each month in Sacramento to execute their duties of oversight, policy setting, and regulation to guide the work of the appointed executive director and Board of Equalization staff. 

Board members are elected to four-year terms in office and cannot serve more than two terms.

Re-elect Sally Lieber to the Board of Equalization to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Sally Lieber has served on the California State Board of Equalization (BOE) since 2023, when she was elected with 70% of the vote. As a member of the board, she has prioritized transparency and accountability, affordable housing, environmental protection, and veterans’ and homeowners’ services. In 2024, Lieber ran an unsuccessful campaign for Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors but was able to retain her BOE seat. She previously served in the California State Assembly, where she championed educational and economic opportunities, environmental protections, and protecting victims and survivors of crime. Lieber has the endorsement of several groups, including Sierra Club, Equality California, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Working Families Party, California Teachers Association, and other labor unions and Democratic Clubs. She also has the support of many elected leaders, such as State Controller Malia Cohen, Attorney General Rob Bonta, Rep. Lateefah Simon, Rep. Elect Sam Sukaton to the Board of Equalization to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Sam Sukaton is lead organizer for AFT Local 1521, the LA Community College Faculty Guild, organizing students and faculty in the largest community college in the district. Elect Tom Umberg to the Board of Equalization to keep California on the right track for progress. 

Sen. Tom Umberg has served in the California State Senate since 2018, and in the State Assembly from 1990–1994 and 2004–2006. Sen. Umberg scores a lifetime 65 out of 100 on Courage Score, our annual analysis of legislators’ progressive voting records. Umberg was deputy drug czar for President Bill Clinton and an assistant United States attorney in Orange County. 

The Race
June 2 primary election results: Denis Bilodeau (R) 45%, Sen. Tom Umberg (D) 21%, Cody Petterson (D) 18%, Martin Arias (D) 14%, and Gardner Osborne (LIB) 2%. Denis Bilodeau and Tom Umberg will contend in the November 3 general election.

Candidate fundraising and pledges: Tom Umberg’s campaign has raised $691,000 and is funded by law enforcement, real estate, and corporate donors. His problematic donors include California Correctional Peace Officers Association, Association of Orange County Deputy Sheriffs, Amazon, and Liberty Mutual Insurance Company. 

Opposing candidate’s fundraising and pledges: Denis Bilodeau’s campaign has raised $135,000 and is funded by real estate interests.

The District
Counties in district: California’s Board of Equalization District 4 includes Imperial, Orange, Riverside, and San Diego Counties.

Voter registration: 39% Democrat, 31% Republican, and 23% No Party Preference. Democrats typically hold this district.

Recent election results: BOE District 4 voted for Kamala Harris for president in 2024 by seven points and Gavin Newsom for governor in 2022 by two points.

The Position
The California Board of Equalization is composed of four members elected by popular vote to represent individual districts within the state. It is the only elected tax board in the country. The state controller serves in an at-large capacity as the 5th member. The Board of Equalization is responsible for managing taxation in the state, including in the areas of property, alcoholic beverage, and insurance. This includes oversight of valuation assessments on public utility and railroad property, mapping and assigning tax rates to geographic areas in the state, conducting assessment surveys and compliance audits, and administering tax exemptions. In California, board members meet each month in Sacramento to execute their duties of oversight, policy setting, and regulation to guide the work of the appointed executive director and Board of Equalization staff. 

Board members are elected to four-year terms in office and cannot serve more than two terms.

Statewide Ballot Measures

Public Transit Revenue Measure

VOTE YES

Public Transit Revenue Measure

VOTE YES ON THE PUBLIC TRANSIT REVENUE MEASURE

California public transportation systems operate on aging infrastructure, and are facing looming service cuts without changes to their funding. The Public Transit Revenue Measure District Proposition RTM would establish a 14-year sales tax to fund Bay Area transit systems, including BART, Caltrain, VTA SamTrans, AC Transit, and Muni. The sales tax would be spread across five counties, with purchases in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties seeing an increase of 0.5%, and purchases in San Francisco County seeing an increase of 1.0%. This tax is estimated to bring in nearly $1 billion annually to support the safety, cleanliness, affordability, and reliability of public transit, and provide some road repairs across the region. 

Why voting YES on the Public Transit Revenue Measure matters:

  • Public transit is critical to the economy of the region, with countless individuals and businesses relying on these systems to ensure their livelihood. Lower post-pandemic ridership has reduced their budgets, and cuts to essential routes and stations are looming. VOTING YES will ensure that these vital transportation systems can continue at current service levels and staffing, and make investments in their systems. 
  • The Public Transit Revenue Measure language includes a build-in for “requiring financial transparency, oversight, and accountability” for the stewardship of the collected sales tax revenue. VOTING YES will approve the collection of these funds with a commitment that each transit system is demonstrating the proper use of the dollars for the benefit of riders and the broader community. 
  • The region already suffers from traffic challenges and high pollution, and nearly half of trips on these transit systems are job-related. Allowing the systems to lose funding and cut service is likely to increase traffic congestion across the area and create more wear and tear on roadways. VOTING YES will ensure that car traffic remains at its current level, and that Californians continue to have extensive opportunities to opt for public transit. 
  • Public transit is a lifeline for vulnerable populations, including lower-income and disabled Californians. VOTING YES will retain travel options and accessibility for these residents and all riders.

Top supporters of the Public Transit Revenue Measure:

  • The Public Transit Revenue Measure has received significant support from organizations within the state, including California Working Families Party, San Francisco Labor Council, National Union of Healthcare Workers, Climate Action California, and YIMBY Action. 
  • It has also received the endorsement of many elected leaders, including Rep. Ro Khanna, State Sen. Scott Wiener, Asm. Ash Kalra, and the mayors of Tracy, Berkeley, Oakland, East Palo Alto, San Francisco, Redwood City, Palo Alto, and Walnut Creek. 
  • Supporters make consistent economic arguments for the value of ensuring that public transportation systems can continue to operate at their current service levels for the benefit of all region residents.

Top opposition to the Public Transit Revenue Measure:

  • The Public Transit Revenue Measure has been opposed by the Committee for Affordable Bay Area Transit, which supports the Fixes Before Funding initiative, and has the support of the Contra Costa Taxpayers Association and the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association. 
  • Those in opposition argue that this sales tax would hit working families hardest in an area that already carries a high cost of living, and that these transit systems have lacked agility in dealing with lower ridership, and the corresponding drop in fare revenue, since 2020. 
  • The opposition also argues that this measure will lock in fixed budget percentages for each transit system, and that the formula will be restrictive and may not allow for funds to flow to the system with the greatest need.

Proposition #1

VOTE YES ON PROP 1

Proposition 1 will authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for the preservation, development, and construction of affordable rental housing, expansion of ownership opportunities for veterans and low-income Californians, and establishment of permanent housing programs for individuals experiencing homelessness. The bonds would provide $6.25 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program (MHP) to build affordable, supportive, and extremely low-income units, and $1.25 billion to the CalVet Home Loan Program to provide reimbursable loans to veterans and their families. Additional bond funds would be delegated to several established state housing programs, including the Portfolio Reinvestment Program, the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program, the Serna Farmworker Housing Program, the Tribal Housing Grant Program, and University of California student housing programs. 

Bonds are a way for the state government to borrow money for up-front funding for projects. Bonds are sold to investors, and the state repays the investors, with interest over time. General obligation bonds are repaid from the state’s General Fund, the main operating account to which revenue from major taxes is directed and from which most state funds are spent. Bond debt repayment uses around 3% of annual General Fund revenues. 

Why voting YES on Proposition 1 matters:

  • While California has prioritized affordable housing development over the last decade, the projects have often relied on one-time investments in a narrow group of programs. For example, the 2018 Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act was exhausted by the end of 2023 due to high demand. VOTING YES on Proposition 1 will create an opportunity for large-scale development and dynamic program investment, allowing the state to keep pace with housing demand and create meaningful opportunities for lower-income rental and ownership. 
  • VOTING YES will create significant economic benefits across the state, including over 50,000 new construction jobs, and $1.3 billion in state and local tax revenue. Generally, state investments in affordable housing can earn up to 300% more in federal, local, and private investment, which provides a significant increase in the efficiency of the public funds. State investments in affordable housing leverage an estimated $4 in federal, local, and private money for every $1 of state funding. 
  • VOTING YES will increase housing availability, and housing stability provides both personal and community benefits. Statistically, young people who grow up in affordable housing see increased median lifetime earnings of $51,000; supportive housing can save a measurable amount of state and local public service funding over time, and strategic building can increase the use of public transit and decrease local emissions.

Top funders of Proposition 1:

  • Proposition 1 has been endorsed by a broad coalition, including Courage California, ACLU California Action, United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America, California Housing Consortium, Disability Rights California, Evolve California, and the League of California Cities. It has also received the support of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Asm. Speaker Robert Rivas, and co-author Asm. Buffy Wicks.
  • The campaign in support of Proposition 1 has received $2.1 million in donations, including from Building a Better California, the San Francisco Foundation, Self-Help Enterprises, and Century Housing Corporation.

Top opposition to Proposition 1:

  • There is no significant statewide opposition to Proposition 1.

Proposition #2

VOTE YES ON PROP 2

For two decades, California has maintained a Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) that serves as a rainy day fund that the state government can use during emergencies or financial crises. Proposition 2, also known as the Save for California’s Future Act, would increase the BSA fund’s cap from 10% to 20% of General Fund revenue. Additionally, Proposition 2 would exclude BSA contributions from the Gann Limit — approved by voters in 1979 — which limits the amount of tax revenue that the state can spend annually. 

Why voting YES on Proposition 2 matters:

  • Since the BSA was established, it has been used to provide statewide support during the pandemic and through difficult budget years. VOTING YES will increase the cap on savings in this account annually, and fortify California against the financial impact of unexpected crises or federal budget cuts in the future. 
  • Federal funding has become increasingly unreliable during the current administration. VOTING YES will ensure that California maintains a larger state-based stockpile of rainy day funds that can be easily accessed during difficult times. 
  • California’s budget has seen unexpected surpluses and deficit swings in recent years, demonstrating significant volatility over time. VOTING YES will allow the state to stabilize its savings and continue to protect critical services, like education and public safety, from unexpected cuts.

Top supporters of Proposition 2:

  • Proposition 2 has the backing of a strong Democratic legislative coalition, including State Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Gov. Gavin Newsom. It has also received the endorsement of the California Democratic Party.

Top opposition to Proposition 2:

  • More fiscally conservative members of the legislature have argued that California has an overspending problem, not a savings problem. This coalition argues that reigning in spending and trimming the budget would be a more sensible solution than increasing savings in the rainy day fund. 
  • Reform California, a right-wing group that is leading statewide efforts to block eligible Californians from voting (including Prop 39) and is backing extremist Republican candidates for office, is a top opponent of Proposition 2.

Proposition #3

VOTE YES ON PROP 3

In 2012, Californians voted to institute higher income tax rates on high earners — single filers with incomes over $250k, or joint filers with incomes above $500k — from 2012 through 2018, providing critical revenue for public K–12 schools and community colleges after years of cuts to public services during the Great Recession. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend the tax through 2030. This year’s Proposition 3 would make the tax permanent, adjust the eligible income brackets, and tie the threshold to inflation. The updated income brackets and their associated rates are:

  • $361,000 to $433,000 (single filer) or $721,000 to $866,000 (joint) at 10.3%
  • $433,000 to $721,000 (single filer) or $866,000 to $1.4 million (joint) at 11.3%
  • Above $721,000 (single filer) or above $1.4 million (joint) at 12.3%

Why voting YES on Proposition 3 matters:

  • The taxes collected through this initiative generate $5 billion to $15 billion annually, totaling about $120 billion since 2012. The funds are redistributed: 89% to K–12 schools and 11% to community colleges. VOTING YES will allow the state to make these budget allocations permanent to continue to provide stable funding to public school systems, which can then invest in valuable academic, social, workforce, and professional programs that create an ongoing benefit to the state’s economy. Additionally, Prop 3 would continue to raise enough revenue to free up General Fund dollars for other public services and purposes. 
  • California is already facing budget deficits, in part because of the deep cuts that Republicans enacted for health care and other critical services in H.R. 1 to subsidize massive tax breaks for the wealthy and corporations. VOTING YES will prevent a significant loss of revenue as federal cuts impact the state and Californians for years. 
  • Proposition 3 continues the existing tax rates without raising them for any individual or household. VOTING YES will maintain the status quo and continue to provide adequate revenue for the state. 
  • This tax only applies to the top 2% of California tax filers and creates an average of $10 billion in revenue annually. These taxes are collected from individuals who have benefitted from California’s resources and infrastructure. VOTING YES ensures that a small portion of that wealth is redistributed to schools and communities to provide similar opportunities to young people. 
  • Failing to renew or make this tax permanent would provide a tax cut exclusive to the top 1%, putting an average of $59,000 back in their pockets annually. This would also mean that the top 1% would have a lower marginal tax rate than the bottom 20%. VOTING YES will ensure that California’s tax system does not regress, and that revenue continues to be available for investment in statewide education programs.

Top supporters of Proposition 3:

  • The Yes on Proposition 3 campaign is led by the Californians for Protecting Public Education, Healthcare, and Budget Stability committee, funded by the California Teachers Association, California Federation of Teachers, and California School Employees Association. The committee collected over 1.6 million signatures to qualify Prop 3 for the ballot. 
  • Prop 3 is endorsed by Courage California, the California Democratic Party, SEIU California, California Professional Firefighters, California Nurses Association, California School Nurses Organization, and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.

Top opposition to Proposition 3:

  • Proposition 3 has been opposed by the California Taxpayers Association, which has argued that making these tax rates permanent strains the state economy by limiting the use of the revenue and deterring investment. 
  • The Pacific Research Institute has argued that removing the expiration date will incentivize high earners and their associated businesses to relocate to states with friendlier tax policy. This response could eventually result in a drop in revenue and the need to find other funding streams to support education initiatives in the state.

Proposition #4

VOTE YES ON PROP 4

Since 2020, over $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races, and wealthy donors and special interests have grown their influence in politics. Public financing of political campaigns would shift power back to everyday voters: candidates would be supported by taxpayer dollars and be more accountable to all residents. 

In 1988, California voters passed Proposition 73 to create a statewide ban on the use of public funding in political campaigns. As a result, only charter cities — cities that are governed by their own local charter (essentially, a local constitution) — have had the authority to provide public campaign financing. Of California’s 483 cities, 121 are charter cities. No other jurisdictions in the state have been permitted to allow the use of public financing. The legislature attempted to override Proposition 73 in 2016, but California law requires that voters participate in the adjustment of any voter-approved initiative. 

Proposition 4 will repeal the 1988 initiative and allow any jurisdiction within the state to pass its own guidelines on the use of public funding in campaigns. Proposition 4 will also require that jurisdictions establish spending limits and criteria for candidates to qualify for public funding, providing substantial guardrails around the practice. 

Why voting YES on Proposition 4 matters:

  • Current campaign-finance laws have resulted in campaigns that are funded largely by super PACs, corporations, and dark money. These interests have an outsized influence on candidates’ policy positions, often outweighing the priorities and needs of voters, and candidates often feel the need to chase these larger-dollar donors to be competitive. VOTING YES will help to even the donor playing field between voters and wealthy interests and establish a viable path for candidates to focus on issues and voter connections instead of spending valuable time fundraising. 
  • Even at the local level, viable campaigns often require a budget that can fund staff, paid media, and other campaign necessities. VOTING YES will allow grassroots candidates with limited resources to receive enough critical funds to launch and sustain a campaign and engage with voters on local issues. 
  • There are several recent, high-profile examples of candidates winning elections against billionaire-funded candidates in charter cities and states where public funding is permitted, including Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. VOTING YES will codify the use of public funds in California elections and provide a pathway to opportunity for more candidates, who better reflect the values and diversity of their communities, to pursue campaigns that could lead to impactful public service. 
  • Oversight of corporate PAC donations is limited, and campaign finance generally lacks transparency. Proposition 4 would require that jurisdictions develop criteria for the distribution of public funds to campaigns, including provisions that prohibit a candidate from using the dollars for legal fees, fines, or repayment of personal loans. VOTING YES will ensure that candidates are vetted, their use of public dollars has guardrails, and data on the use of public funds is available to voters. 
  • California currently has five charter cities that have adopted public campaign funding initiatives: Berkeley, Long Beach, Los Angeles, Oakland, and San Francisco. VOTING YES will ensure that all jurisdictions in California can benefit from this model if they decide to pursue it.

Top supporters of Proposition 4:

  • Proposition 4 has been endorsed by many good governance and progressive groups, including Courage California, California Clean Money Action Fund, California Common Cause, League of Women Voters California, End Citizens United, ACLU of California, California Working Families Party, California Environmental Voters, California Federation of Labor Unions, and Progressive Democrats of America-California.
  • Supporters view this initiative as an opportunity to reduce the influence of Big Money, increase the availability of politics to more voters and candidates, and improve the accessibility of elections.

Top opposition to Proposition 4:

  • This initiative is opposed by the California Taxpayers Association, which objects to the use of public tax dollars to further boost the financial integrity of elections. They argue that elections do not carry the same neutrality as other tax-funded initiatives, like schools, libraries, and infrastructure, and that taxpayers cannot universally agree on the funding of individual candidates and platforms.

  • Proposition 4 has been endorsed by many good governance and progressive groups, including Courage California, California Clean Money Action Fund, California Common Cause, League of Women Voters California, End Citizens United, ACLU of California, California Working Families Party, California Environmental Voters, California Federation of Labor Unions, and Progressive Democrats of America-California.
  • Supporters view this initiative as an opportunity to reduce the influence of Big Money, increase the availability of politics to more voters and candidates, and improve the accessibility of elections.

Top opposition to Proposition 4:

  • This initiative is opposed by the California Taxpayers Association, which objects to the use of public tax dollars to further boost the financial integrity of elections. They argue that elections do not carry the same neutrality as other tax-funded initiatives, like schools, libraries, and infrastructure, and that taxpayers cannot universally agree on the funding of individual candidates and platforms.

Proposition #5

VOTE YES ON PROP 5

The California Constitution allows voters to recall elected statewide officials prior to the end of their term through a special recall election. Currently, special recall elections are accompanied by a simultaneous election to replace the recalled officer. Proposition 5 would amend this process by eliminating the same-day election to replace a recalled candidate. Instead, voters would decide on whether or not to recall a statewide officer in one election, and a replacement would be chosen by either a later special election, a gubernatorial appointment, or the next general election. Proposition 5 would allow the recalled officer to run again for the same seat, but would not permit them to be appointed back to the seat. 

Proposition 5 includes a carve-out for the recall of a sitting governor. Under that situation, the lieutenant governor would serve either the remainder of the term or until a special election to replace the governor could be scheduled, depending on when the recall occurred during the term.

Why voting YES on Proposition 5 matters:

  • The current process of recalling and replacing during a single election can incentivize bad actors to pursue the removal of a public official while pushing forward a replacement candidate who would be unlikely to win a nomination under normal circumstances. Voter turnout in special recall elections is significantly lower than a regular primary or general election, so a less qualified or politically appealing candidate can often win the election without weathering a typical campaign cycle. VOTING YES will remove the advantage for these bad actors and require that anyone seeking to replace a recalled candidate must go through a special or general election campaign cycle. 
  • Existing law does not allow a recalled candidate to run for their seat again, even if their recall has been devised and executed by a small group of motivated petitioners. VOTING YES will diminish the benefit to recall advocates by ensuring that a recalled official can run again for their seat and ultimately allowing the broader voting population to determine their fitness for office. 
  • Recall elections are sometimes abused as a tool for political gamesmanship, allowing for the strategic removal of someone who has won a fair election, often by the people and interests who opposed the candidate in the original election. VOTING YES will limit the ways in which this tool can be weaponized and better protect the foundation of fair elections and representation that is essential to our democratic system. 
  • Taxpayers bear the costs of recall elections, which are administered through the state and county elections offices. The failed 2021 recall election of Governor Newsom cost taxpayers over $200 million – nearly $175 million from counties and $26 million from the state. VOTING YES will reform the process to potentially reduce the number of recall special elections and save taxpayer dollars.

Top supporters of Proposition 5:

  • Proposition 5 is supported by California Common Cause and League of Women Voters of California, who argue that the current recall election ballots are worded in ways that can confuse voters. They view Proposition 5 as a way to streamline the process and ensure that voters have the opportunity to select their preferred replacement through later elections. 
  • SCA 1, the legislation that resulted in Proposition 5, was authored by Sen. Josh Newman and Asm. Isaac Bryan. They argued that the current model allows a replacement candidate with less than the majority of votes to take office, which is not permitted in any other state elections. Newman, a Democrat, was elected to the state Senate in 2016, then recalled and replaced by a Republican in 2018. He regained his seat in the 2020 election.

Top opposition to Proposition 5:

  • Election Integrity Project California — a right-wing group founded by a former tea party activist and with ties to the Republican Party — has opposed Proposition 5 under the argument that allowing a lieutenant governor to replace a governor would not provide voters with a leader who has a different political identity or policy views. This demonstrates the standard misuse of recall elections as a means to switch the party affiliation of the person in office or to create a shortcut to Republican leadership after a loss in a fair election.

Proposition #37

No Position

Proposition #37

VOTE YOUR VALUES ON PROP 37

In recent decades, California’s extensive housing issues have included challenges of affordability, availability, and insurability, making long-term homeownership increasingly difficult for many residents. Proposition 37 seeks to address that issue by allowing qualified homebuyers to access a $25 billion bond fund — administered by the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) — to set up a second mortgage. To qualify for this program, a homebuyer would need to have been a California resident for at least one year, have an income at or below 200% of the median income for a family in the area of the home purchase, occupy the home as a primary residence, and make a down payment of at least 3%. The measure would offer a fixed-rate mortgage of the purchase price for homes under $1.5 million, and would require that the purchased home be newly constructed houses, townhomes, rowhouses, condominiums, or manufactured homes. 

Homebuyers are generally required to make a 20% down payment to purchase a home. The remaining 80% of the purchase price is secured through a 15- or 30-year mortgage loan. Proposition 37 would help qualified homebuyers who can make at least a 3% down payment secure a second fixed-rate mortgage loan for the up to 17% difference in down payment. According to Zillow, the average cost of a single family home in California is $773,000. Covering 3% of a down payment on a home of this price would require savings of $23,000. Thus, Proposition 37 is a narrow pathway to homeownership that will only be viable for a limited number of Californians. 

Top supporters of Proposition 37:

  • Primary support has been organized through the California Coalition for Homeownership, and backers include the California Democratic Party and California Association of Realtors. Proposition 37 is also supported by Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Beccera, Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond, and former Rep. Katie Porter. They argue that this program will increase housing affordability for middle class and first-time homebuyers. 
  • Proposition 37 also has the support of several carpentry unions, which stand to see work and economic benefits for their members if new housing construction is increased across the state.

Top opposition to Proposition 37:

  • There has been no organized public opposition to Proposition 37 as of summer 2026.

Proposition #38

VOTE NO ON PROP 38

Proposition 38 will authorize an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy, with $4.2 billion to be directed to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII). CIII is a research institute co-founded by the billionaire backers of this proposition, Dr. Gary Michelson and Meyer Luskin. Michelson is the chairman of the CIII board of directors, and Luskin is the treasurer. CIII received $200 million in start-up funding from the state, and is currently being built on the University of California, Los Angeles campus. The remaining $4.2 billion would be distributed across non-profit universities and medical research institutes through a competitive grant process that CIII would participate in, and grantees would be required to collaborate with CIII on clinical trials funded by the bond. 

The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) estimates that repayment of this bond fund will increase state costs by $500 million to $600 million annually for the next 20 years. Any resulting technology or medical therapies developed from the research funded through Proposition 38 would be sold at 20% lower than the national average, providing some benefit back to taxpayers. 

Why voting NO on Proposition 38 matters:

  • California is home to many established, top immunology research institutions. VOTING NO will stop two billionaires from steering $4.2 billion in state funds to their own research institute that is not currently operational and lacks an institutional research track record. 
  • The state is already facing budget deficits and funding shortages, largely due to the significant federal H.R. 1 cuts to Medi-Cal, CalFresh, and other critical programs. VOTING NO on Prop 38 will save the state from having to divert $500 million to $600 million in state funding each year from critical health and human services to bond repayment. 
  • This year, the California state legislature passed the California Science and Health Research Bond Act, a $7.5 billion bond that will be on the March 2028 statewide ballot if signed by the governor by September 30. VOTING NO on Prop 38 will allow voters to approve a more equitable and transparent bond than Prop 38.

Top opposition to Proposition 38:

  • The No on 38 campaign is led by Dr. Robert Kaplan, a senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health. Prop 38 is also opposed by Courage California, League of Women Voters of California, and former Legislative Analyst’s Office analysts.

Top supporters of Proposition 38:

  • Proposition 38 is supported by the Yes on 38 committee and Californians for Life-Saving Immunology Research & Cures, and it has the endorsement of ALS Association, Alzheimer’s Association, American Nurses Association of California, California Black Health Network, and Parkinson Association of Northern California. 
  • Dr. Michelson and his affiliated Michelson Center for Public Policy have contributed $22 million to support Prop 38, and Luskin has given $5 million.

Proposition #39

VOTE NO ON PROP 39

To register to vote, California law requires verification of their citizenship status, residency, and eligibility to vote with their date of birth, a government-issued identification, and the last four digits of their Social Security Number. Proposition 39 is a MAGA-led effort to amend the California Constitution to also require verification at the point of voting — voters would have to either list the last four digits of their government-issued ID on the outside of their mail-in ballot envelope or present those IDs to cast an in-person ballot. This measure would also require the state to provide free voter-identification cards to voters, require election officials to complete an annual citizenship-verification process on their voter rolls using available government data, report on the percentage of voters who have been citizenship verified annually, require the state auditor to report on government compliance every two years, and require the state legislature to pass additional laws. 

Why voting NO on Proposition 39 matters:

  • California exceeds federal requirements for election security. California already requires ID verification during the registration process, and includes a signed citizenship attestation under penalty of perjury. Asking registered voters to complete this process again is intentionally designed to make it harder for people to vote, and VOTING NO will ensure that California continues to be a leading state on making voting more accessible for all eligible residents. 
  • Requiring point-of-voting ID verification is going to create challenges for already disadvantaged groups, including low-income individuals who can’t afford to maintain a state-issued ID, individuals whose address does not match their ID due to instability of housing or displacement, and individuals who do not maintain a physical copy of their birth certificate or Social Security card. Data shows that young and Latino Californians would be most impacted by these barriers. VOTING NO will prevent the state from disenfranchising a registered voter if they cannot produce a document on demand.
  • National and state data continues to show that voter fraud is extremely rare, making up a fraction of a percentage point of overall voting in the United States. VOTING NO will ensure that California does not waste millions of dollars and disenfranchise eligible voters in an effort to solve a problem that does not exist. 
  • Proposition 39 includes administrative requirements of annual citizenship verification and state audit compliance reports, free voter-identification cards, and potential additional costs determined by the state legislature. These efforts are estimated to cost the state tens of millions of dollars in an already tight state budget. VOTING NO will ensure that California does not need to allocate significant funds for ongoing and duplicative voter-verification efforts.

Top opposition to Proposition 39:

  • Proposition 39 is opposed by the California Democratic Party, ACLU, California Common Cause, League of Women Voters California, Planned Parenthood, California Teachers Association, California Nurses Association, SEIU California, United Domestic Workers, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla, Xavier Becerra, and democratic leaders across the state. Courage California sits on the California for Voting Rights committee in opposition. 
  • Opponents view this conservative effort as a local attempt to seed the Trump administration’s election denialism within the state’s voting infrastructure, and argue that it would intimidate voters and reject legitimate ballots.

Top supporters of Proposition 39:

  • Proposition 39 was led in the legislature by two MAGA Republican members, Asm. Carl DeMaio and Sen. Tony Strickland, and has the endorsement of the California Republican Party. Notably, Republicans have not had a voter registration advantage in the state for decades, and have led multiple efforts to keep eligible Californians — especially residents from communities that tend to lean toward Democrats — from voting. 
  • Supporters argue that presenting ID at the polls is standard practice in many countries, and that around half of other U.S. states require it. They claim the requirement is common sense, but election experts agree that policies like Prop 39 make it harder for people to vote and contribute to election outcomes that do not reflect the diversity of voters.
